verses.1: Al-Mizan takes the verse to forbid certain emigrant believers from secretly communicating friendship to the Meccan polytheists in order to protect relatives and children left in Mecca. It reports that the occasion was Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a's letter informing the Meccans of the Prophet's intended march, sent to obtain leverage for his family; the report corroborates, rather than replaces, the verse's indication. The enemies are plural in sense from the surrounding plurals: they are God's enemies through associationism, rejection of His call, and denial of His Messenger, and the believers' enemies because they persecuted faith and its sacrifices. Mentioning both enmities intensifies the prohibition. Their expulsion of the Messenger and believers means compelling their migration because they believed in their Lord, a true and obligatory matter rather than an offence. The reference to emigration for striving and seeking God's pleasure makes an already realized condition serve as emphatic rebuke: one who has emigrated for that end cannot befriend these enemies. Secretly confiding friendship is disclosing what is inwardly concealed, while God's knowledge makes concealment and declaration alike; the alternative grammatical reading of a'lamu as simply I know does not alter this force. Such support for them is straying from the straight path, God's path.
verses.2: Al-Mizan says the verse removes the assumption that secret friendship could win protection or extinguish the Meccan polytheists' enmity. Thaqf may denote skilled finding or gaining mastery; in this context, victory is especially suitable, though the two meanings are close. If they gain dominance, they will remain enemies: extending their hands means killing, capture, persecution, and torture, and extending their tongues means curses and abuse. Their wish for believers' disbelief is part of the conditional outcome, expressing the same aim that governed their earlier Meccan persecution. Thus accommodation would not secure friendship; it would leave believers exposed to coercion intended to make them renounce religion.
verses.3: Al-Mizan treats this as the answer to the excuse for befriending the Meccan polytheists: the emigrants hoped thereby to protect relatives and children left among them. On the Day of Resurrection those relatives will not avert the punishment incurred by such treachery. The preferred meaning of God's separating people is that the worldly causal ties of kinship are cut when realities are uncovered. Kinship produces mercy, affection, mutual help, tribal solidarity, and service only within social life and its conventional assumptions; when those assumptions fall away, its independent efficacy also vanishes, as in (23:101), (6:94), and (2:166). Therefore no one should endanger himself before God and His Messenger for relations that cannot save him then. The reading that the horrors make people flee from one another is possible, but contextually weaker. The readings that separation means dividing believers from unbelievers, or judgment between disputants, are likewise unsuitable because the verse supplies neither the relatives' disbelief nor a dispute. God's seeing all deeds confirms that neither the act nor its motive escapes recompense.
verses.4:
Al-Mizan presents Abraham and those with him as the model for believers facing idolatrous opponents. Their dissociation is not merely verbal: they reject their people's worship in deed, oppose it inwardly with enmity and hatred, and resolve to maintain that separation until the people believe in God alone. The enduring enmity therefore concerns their polytheism, not an unrestricted personal hostility.

The exception concerning Abraham's promise to seek forgiveness for his father does not qualify that stance as friendship. Abraham made it while hoping for his father's repentance; when his entrenched enmity to God became known, he dissociated himself, as (9:114) states. His words in (19:47-48) join the promise with withdrawal from the father and his worship, showing that the promise was neither endorsement nor a breach of dissociation. Al-Mizan records both grammatical possibilities: it may be a connected exception, since the promise is the one statement not itself dissociation, or an unconnected exception, because it preceded Abraham's final dissociation. In either case, the required exemplar is his dissociation, not the promise of forgiveness.

His admission that he owns nothing for his father from God safeguards the point: prayer is a needy servant's request of the Lord, not a claim of independent power over divine forgiveness. Al-Mizan likens this corrective acknowledgement to Shu'ayb's disclaimer of independent success in (11:88). The prayer that follows is itself part of the example. Having broken their worldly ties, Abraham and his companions entrust their affairs to God, turn back to Him, and recognize that every deed and doer returns to Him. Tawakkul is thus handing over the management of affairs to God, and inaba is the return by which they abandon self-management for Him.
verses.5: Al-Mizan reads the prayer as a request for protection from the consequences of dissociating from unbelievers and for forgiveness. Fitna means that by which one is tested; the believers ask not to be made such a test by being placed under disbelievers' power, which would enable the latter to corrupt and harm them because of their faith and rejection of idols. Repeatedly saying our Lord invokes mercy. The appeal to the Mighty and Wise means that God is unconquered and perfectly acts with knowledge: He can protect them from His enemies' plots and knows how to do so.
verses.6: Al-Mizan says the verse repeats Abraham's exemplary status to secure an affirmative response from those who hope in God and the Last Day. They are to imitate both his dissociation from disbelievers and his humble supplication. Hoping in God means desiring His reward through faith, and hoping in the Last Day means desiring the promised reward, which is equivalent to faith. Whoever refuses gains nothing against God: He needs neither obedience nor compliance with this command. His praiseworthiness lies in commands and prohibitions directed solely to human rectification and a blessed, happy life.
verses.7: Al-Mizan identifies those formerly opposed as the Meccan disbelievers and interprets the promised love as their being granted tawfiq to accept Islam, producing reconciliation, as occurred through the conquest of Mecca. It is not an abrogation of dissociation while they remain polytheists. The verse therefore directs believers to hope that God's power, forgiveness, and mercy will turn this enmity into friendship when they repent and submit to Him.
verses.8: Al-Mizan explains (60:8) and the following verse as defining the scope of the opening prohibition. It concerns neither every non-Muslim nor those who neither fought believers on account of religion nor expelled them, including peaceful treaty partners. Birr, ihsan, and qist require civil, kind, and just dealing, and God's love of the just supplies the reason for permitting it. The verse is not abrogated by (9:5): its own scope is protected non-Muslims and those under treaty, whereas (9:5) concerns polytheists at war. Since the two verses address different cases, there is no contradiction for abrogation to resolve.
verses.9: Al-Mizan identifies those whom (60:9) forbids believers to take as allies as the Meccan polytheists who fought them over religion, expelled them, or aided that expulsion. The wording makes alliance with precisely that hostile group the prohibited matter. Those who form such alliances, including with their supporters against Muslims, are the wrongdoers because they disobey this prohibition. The judgment does not encompass believers who maintain the civil and just dealings with non-hostile disbelievers permitted in the preceding verse; alternatively, the closing description reinforces the prohibition itself.
verses.10:
Al-Mizan relates the verse to the Treaty of Hudaybiyya: its return condition concerned Meccan men who emigrated to Medina, not women. When a Meccan woman embraced Islam and emigrated, the Prophet did not return her to her disbelieving husband, but repaid the dower; the verse legislates this case and its counterparts. Calling the arrivals believing women initially reflects their outward profession. The commanded examination is by evidence such as the shahada or an oath sufficient for ordinary knowledge and trust, while God alone knows faith's reality.

Once they are known as believers, they are not returned. Their faith is the reason both for that judgment and for severing the marriage bond: the two clauses of non-lawfulness establish the termination of marriage, not a wider prohibition. The former husband receives the dower he paid, and a Muslim man may marry the woman after giving her her due, here also her dower. Conversely, a Muslim who has embraced Islam must not retain the permanent marital bond with a disbelieving wife, whether polytheist or from the People of the Book. Al-Mizan recalls its earlier conclusion that this does not abrogate either (2:221) or (5:5).

The reciprocal rule is financial: Muslim husbands may claim what they spent when wives join the disbelievers, and disbelieving husbands may claim the dower when wives join Muslims. These are God's legislated judgments between the parties, issued by the Knowing and Wise.
verses.11: Al-Mizan takes the thing lost when a wife passes to the unbelievers to be her dower. Fawt denotes something becoming remote and hard to recover. The preferred explanation of fa'aqabtum is that believers subsequently obtain war booty from the disbelievers, the outcome of a raid; proposed derivations from following after or a turn are noted but do not govern the explanation. If a Muslim wife joins the disbelievers and her husband cannot recover what he paid, then when such booty comes, he is to receive an equivalent amount. Al-Mizan sets aside several readings it judges remote from the normal sense. The final command of taqwa follows from faith itself: believing in God necessarily entails being careful of one's duty to Him.
verses.12:
Al-Mizan describes this as God's ruling on the believing women's pledge. It includes obligations shared with men, above all abandoning associationism and obeying the Messenger in what is good, and obligations especially addressed to women because of their place in household management, chastity, lineage, and legitimate birth, while allowing that several also concern both sexes. The conditional premise lists the pledge and its result is that the Prophet accepts it and seeks God's forgiveness for them.

They must not associate idols or other gods with God; steal, particularly as the context suggests from husbands but also from anyone; take lovers; kill children by burial alive, other killing, or abortion; or invent the distinct calumny of attributing an adulterously conceived child to the husband. The latter comes from between their hands and feet because that is where the child emerges; its separate mention is not redundant with the prohibition of adultery. Disobeying the Prophet in what is good means falling short of the Prophetic practices and teachings established in the Muslim society, whether by omitting obligations such as prayer and alms or committing prohibitions such as pre-Islamic display. The closing description of God as Forgiving and Merciful makes forgiveness necessary in meaning and strengthens hope.
verses.13: Al-Mizan identifies the people under God's wrath as the Jews, distinguishing them from the disbelievers mentioned at the verse's end. Their despair concerns the reward of the Hereafter. The likened disbelievers are, primarily, those who deny God and resurrection and therefore despair of the dead in the graves; the report that it means specifically the Meccan polytheists is also noted. The verse warns believers against friendship and mixing by declaring the Jews' enduring deprivation and ruin. It also records two less-preferred alternatives: disbelievers may mean those who bury and conceal the dead, from the root sense of kufr, or the dead disbelievers themselves, with min specifying their kind, as supported by (2:161).
